Latin-anon here. My non-machine translation:

“May the morning [star] Lucifer find his flames. That Lucifer, I say, who does not know Christ Your Son, [Christ] who, having returned from Hell, became a clear dawn for human kind and lives and reigns forever and ever.”

This is not what you think it is. It is NOT an invocation of the devil, rather a condemnation of him. It asking (in the subjunctive) from God the Father, that the devil (Lucifer, the morning star) may meet (inveniat) his damnation (in flames, flammas). It then goes on to say that Lucifer does not know (i.e. accept) Christ, Christ who rose from the dead (regressus ab infernis) and became the salvation (or light, from illuxit) for mankind.

As for translating this passage, the key here is to follow the relative pronouns to see who is the antecedent, i.e. who is being referred to by “qui.” However this passage is not particularly difficult for those with experience translating prose like Cicero or poetry like Virgil or Ovid.

Many of the phrases used here contain meanings first established in the Classical period of Latin, in the times of Cicero and Virgil. “Lucifer” literally means “light-bearer” and in pre-Christian eras was the proper name for a particular star that rises in the morning. “Lucifer matutinus” means “morning star.” “Serenus illuxit” carries a literal meaning of a dawn with clear skies. Referring to Christ as becoming a “clear dawn” (Serenus illuxit in it’s literal translation) for mankind connotes a supplantation of Lucifer as the true light that breaks the darkness of night. “Ille” has the connotation of meaning “that well-known man,” or here being “that infamous Lucifer.” “Inquam” also denotes an affirmation of the supplicant in asking God for this petition in addition to its literal meaning of “I say.”

There is a lot here as Latin is a language with a lot of history coloring the words with a poetic meaning. Many Classical Latin references carry over to Ecclesiastical Latin as the words and structures have become inextricable from historical and poetic references. I can go on for quite a while. Needless to say, Latin can be indecipherable for both machines and those with little Classical training. Ancient languages are tricky like that. It is hard to avoid the temptation to rush to conclusions, especially if one has just enough knowledge to be dangerous. Machine translations of Latin are for the most part useless.
